preamble: Deaspiration of [kʰ] to plain [k]. The classic case is Grassmann's law in Ancient Greek, a dissimilation in which the first of two aspirates in successive syllables loses its aspiration; it is most visible in reduplicated perfects, where the reduplicating syllable of a χ-initial root surfaces with κ. Independently, Sinhala lost the aspiration contrast altogether, so inherited Indo-Aryan kh became k. In Sanskrit reduplication kh is also deaspirated, but the reduplicant is additionally palatalized to c, so Sanskrit belongs to a different cell. In the Nguni languages Xhosa and Zulu, [kʰ] loses its aspiration after a non-syllabic homorganic nasal, most visibly in class 9/10 nouns formed with the prefix iN- (Zulu khumbula 'to remember' > inkumbulo 'memory'); Wikipedia's prenasalisation tables label the rule "Aspiration is lost on obstruents". Zulu realizes the resulting plain stop as an ejective, while Xhosa ejectives tend to be tenuis stops except in careful pronunciation or salient positions (Wikipedia, Xhosa language).

examples.note: Grassmann's law: the reduplicating syllable loses its aspiration before the aspirated root-initial χ.
Same deaspiration of the reduplicant; participle κεχηνώς.
Sinhala lost the aspiration contrast in plosives; compare Hindustani khānā, which keeps kh.
The Middle Indo-Aryan kh from the kṣ cluster (Pali khīra) appears as plain k; cognate Dhivehi kiru.
